Possible GRIM inconsistencies

Source: R/grim-stats.R
grim-stats.Rd

These functions quantify how informative a GRIM test is for a given sample size and number of decimal places:

  • grim_exp_incon() returns the probability that a mean or percentage with digits_x random decimal digits is GRIM-inconsistent with n. It is the exp_incon column of grim_map().

  • grim_total() returns the number of such inconsistent values between two whole numbers, out of 10^digits_x (10^(digits_x + 2) with x_meaning = "percentage").

See vignette("grim-in-depth"), section GRIM statistics.

Usage

grim_exp_incon(
  x,
  n,
  digits_x,
  items_averaged,
  data_type,
  x_meaning = c("mean", "percentage"),
  rounding = "up_or_down",
  threshold = 5,
  percent = deprecated()
)

grim_total(
  x,
  n,
  digits_x,
  items_averaged,
  data_type,
  x_meaning = c("mean", "percentage"),
  rounding = "up_or_down",
  threshold = 5,
  percent = deprecated()
)

Arguments

x

Numeric. The mean or percentage. Only whether it is missing or infinite matters; the argument mirrors grim().

n

Integer. The sample size.

digits_x

Integer. The number of decimal places in x, including trailing zeros. There is no default, since a numeric value does not keep them (1.40 is 1.4).

items_averaged

Integer. As in grim().

data_type

String. As in grim(). No default. For "continuous" data, which GRIM can't find inconsistent, the result is 0, or NA where grim() is NA.

x_meaning

String. "mean" (the default) or "percentage", which adds 2 to the decimal count, as in grim().

rounding, threshold

As in grim(). The count depends on the method; "even" counts a tie on either bound as consistent, as grim() does. grim_map() passes its own on.

percent

Replaced by x_meaning: use x_meaning = "percentage" instead of percent = TRUE.

Value

Double. For integer data, grim_exp_incon() and grim_total() return NA if x is missing or infinite, if digits_x is missing, or if n or items_averaged is missing or not a positive whole number. These include every case that grim() cannot decide, and some that it can: a mean may pass whatever n is, but how many fail depends on it. For continuous data, they return 0, or NA where grim() is NA. Under data_type = NA, they return NA unless the count is 0. A count above 2^53, which only digits_x of 14 or more with x_meaning = "percentage" can reach, is the nearest number a double can hold.

Details

x, n, digits_x, items_averaged, and data_type are recycled to a common length by the tidyverse rules: an argument has length 1 or the length of the longest.

References

Brown, N. J. L., & Heathers, J. A. J. (2017). The GRIM Test: A Simple Technique Detects Numerous Anomalies in the Reporting of Results in Psychology. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 8(4), 363–369. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1948550616673876

See also

grim() and grim_map().

Examples

# Many value sets are inconsistent here:
grim_exp_incon(
  x = 83.29,
  n = 21,
  digits_x = 2,
  items_averaged = 1,
  data_type = "integer"
)
#> [1] 0.79
grim_total(
  x = 83.29,
  n = 21,
  digits_x = 2,
  items_averaged = 1,
  data_type = "integer"
)
#> [1] 79

# None are in this case...
grim_exp_incon(
  x = 5.14,
  n = 120,
  digits_x = 2,
  items_averaged = 1,
  data_type = "integer"
)
#> [1] 0
grim_total(
  x = 5.14,
  n = 120,
  digits_x = 2,
  items_averaged = 1,
  data_type = "integer"
)
#> [1] 0

# ...but most would be if `x` were a percentage:
grim_exp_incon(
  x = 5.14,
  n = 120,
  digits_x = 2,
  items_averaged = 1,
  data_type = "integer",
  x_meaning = "percentage"
)
#> [1] 0.988
grim_total(
  x = 5.14,
  n = 120,
  digits_x = 2,
  items_averaged = 1,
  data_type = "integer",
  x_meaning = "percentage"
)
#> [1] 9880
